beats.line: This planet goes the wrong way around its star.

Almost every other world in the galaxy turns the same direction.
This one runs backwards.

It was never made here.
It was thrown, or captured, or flung into this orbit.

There is no ordinary reason for a world to turn against its star.
Whatever put it here left it there.

Now look at how little of it is actually there.
It is one of the puffiest planets we have ever measured.

So low in density that it floats like a cork.
A world the size of Jupiter, made of almost nothing.

It should have collapsed into itself a long time ago.
The heat down inside holds it open. That is all.

Its clouds stack so high they look like a wall of weather.
And the wind in them never stops.

The whole atmosphere just runs, endlessly, around the day side.
Those clouds move faster than anything that size should.
The side facing the star hits seventeen hundred degrees.

You would not land here.
You would not orbit here.
You would not want to fall asleep here.

Backwards spin. Almost no weight. Endless wind.
A planet that lost its place and never noticed.
Every part of it is wrong.

You are looking at a world nobody planned.
It is still there. It is still turning.
It was never supposed to be here.

beats.line: You know how a hurricane shoves you flat across open ground. Remember that. It is nothing.
This is WASP-127b. A gas giant, far too close to its own star. And it is almost nothing.
The fastest winds ever measured on an exoplanet. Thousands of kilometers per hour, hour after hour.
They cross the entire planet without ever touching down anywhere. Nothing like that should hold together.
And inside all that fury, the planet is almost empty. One of the lowest densities ever measured.
A giant with nothing inside it, screaming at thousands of kilometers per hour. You cannot stand on that.
So you do what astronomers do. You read the star's light instead of standing out in the wind.
You map the atmosphere by watching which colors of starlight get swallowed on the way in.
Whatever colors are missing, exactly, tell you what is standing up there in the dark.
Water. Leaving. Upward, fast, and not falling back down. Just going out, past the edge of everything.
And a thin haze of small grains, floating far too high above the top of the cloud deck.
That is not a planet holding its air. That is a planet throwing it away.
The air does not come back. Your sky has a leak, and that leak has no bottom at all.
You are watching it from far too away to help. That is the whole story of this world.

beats.line:
Here is a planet made of ice.
And it is on fire, and it does not melt.
This is Gliese 436 b.

It is about the size of Neptune.
A giant world, made almost entirely of water.

Now here is the part that makes no sense.
Ice should melt. That is what ice does.

But this ice is under crushing pressure from its own gravity.
And its star keeps cooking it from close range.
All of that pressure and heat at once.

The water never gets to choose.
It cannot be solid. It cannot be liquid.
It is something in between.

Scientists call it supercritical.
A supercritical fluid. No boundary between ice and steam.

Imagine ice that flows like water and burns like a torch.
That is the surface of this world.
You could not stand on it. You could not swim in it.
It would eat through your ship.

And this world is not alone out here.
It has lost a lot of mass over its life.
Hydrogen and helium are escaping from it, right now.

They stream away in a long comet-like tail.
And that tail glows. It glows in the dark.

So picture a burning-ice planet dragging a glowing tail of gas behind it.
A hot, dense, impossible world, screaming around its star.
It is one of the strangest things in the galaxy.
And it is just sitting there. Burning its ice. Quietly. Forever.

beats.line: This planet sits closer to its star than any planet we have found.

One year up there lasts about five hours and forty minutes.
Sunrise, noon, sunset, gone. Over and over.

The star swings around again before this sentence ends.
Its whole life happens inside one breath of yours.

It is a bare rock. No air. No ocean. No weather.
Nothing there has been alive in a very long while.
Just a charred shell with a dead core inside.

Its star is enormous, and close, and very hot.
It has been boiling this rock since they formed.
Whatever atmosphere it ever had was taken off years ago.

The surface has been melted, drained, hardened again.
It is a cinder. The catalog has nothing closer.

Kepler only ever saw a shadow. Every five hours, forty minutes.
It dipped, and the star dimmed, and dipped again.
KOI-55 is a number. Nobody gave it a better name.

It is falling inward, one orbit at a time.
Every pass takes it closer to the surface.
There is nothing left underneath to fall toward.

Here is the part that should keep you awake.
This world may already have been swallowed once.
It may already have survived being eaten.

That is what makes it disturbing. Not that it dies.
That it is allowed to die twice.

The next pass will not be a pass.
It will be the last one.

KOI-55. Five hours and forty minutes a year.
One fall left. Nothing is coming back.

beats.line:
Some planets swallow the light that reaches them.
This one hands it back.

LTT 9779 b is a super-Earth with a permanent gleam.
Its star is quiet. Dim. Easy to overlook.

The planet is not easy to overlook.
It sits close in, and it never gets the chance to cool down.

High above the surface, the sky is made of metal.
Clouds of metal, miles up, doing nothing useful.

The dayside is irradiated. Continuously. Without pause.
Yet the surface never cooks.

Almost none of that light is absorbed.
Nearly all of it is reflected straight back into space.

From a distance, the planet glows like a coin in the dark.
Not a coal. A mirror.

Astronomers measured the brightness and did not believe it.
A number that high usually means a mistake.

They checked. It is one of the most reflective worlds known.
The night side stays dark. The day side burns.

That is the unsettling part.
The hottest worlds should look like ovens.

This one looks like it is smiling.
It orbits a star so mild it barely deserves the name.

And still the planet comes back brilliant.
No surface you could stand on. No sky you could breathe.

You would not survive a single breath up there.
Nothing down there generates its own shine.

It is the brightest warning light in a quiet system.
The gleam is borrowed. And it never stops.

beats.line: Fomalhaut is the brightest star in the autumn sky, easy to spot and impossible to forget.
Around it lies a ring. A wide, thin belt of dust and ice, far past where any planet should be.
In 2008, something inside that ring caught the light and held it.
The first planet ever imaged in visible light around a star that was not our Sun.
That was the headline. The whole field sat back, because that was supposed to be the end of the argument.
It was not the end. The signal is so faint that some astronomers still call it a dust cloud.
Just dust, kicked up by something invisible passing through the ring on its way out.
Or a real world, shepherding the ring, holding that whole belt in its gravity.
Same light. Same picture. Two entirely different things, and no telescope alive can tell them apart.
Then there is the orbit. It swings in close to the star, then throws itself far out into the cold.
An ellipse that wild does not stay tidy for long.
One bad pass, one nudge from that star, and it never comes back around.
So the likeliest ending is a long, silent fall out of the system, with nothing left to catch it.
The first planet we ever saw in visible light. Maybe a cloud. Maybe a world. Maybe already gone.

beats.line:
This is the hottest planet ever found.
It is hotter than most stars in the galaxy.
Not a little hotter. Considerably hotter.

Even the word planet feels like rounding it up.
Its name is KELT plus nine b.

It circles closer than any planet should.
One year there lasts about a day and a half.

Nothing about the arrangement is survivable for long.
The sunrise there happens once every day and a half.
Because it never turns its back on the star.

The star it rides is a blue furnace, spinning fast.
Up there it is hotter than the planet it made.
The planet is cooking in a light most stars never give.

Its dayside reaches about forty-six hundred degrees.
That is not a temperature. That is a warning.

Hydrogen molecules get torn apart before they can settle.
Its atmosphere is pulled apart and dragged off into space.
It leaves a glowing tail, forever losing weight.

Here is the part that should stop you.
On the dayside, atoms begin to come undone.

The bonds that make matter simply lose.
This is a planet disassembling itself in plain view.
The night side is almost gentle by comparison.
One half of it survives. The other half does not.

And there is nowhere cooler to stand.
No ocean. No shade. No door.
Just a point you would call a star from far off.

You would call it a planet. You would be generous.
Somewhere out there, right now, it is happening.

beats.line:
Every planet you have met so far had a sun.
A star to rise into, and set behind.

This one lost all of that.
Something kicked it out of its system.
A neighbor, moving too close, too fast.

Thrown loose into the dark between the stars.
It has been falling ever since.

It drifts through interstellar space, and nothing slows it.
No star to orbit.
No sunrise. No sunset. Nothing to rise or set.

No light of its own.
It is only ever lit by what other stars leak.

A thin drizzle of scattered light, from impossibly far away.
Barely enough to see by.
Barely enough for anyone to be seen.

This is what it means to be a rogue planet.
No parent star. No system. No address at all.

Among the coldest objects we have ever measured.
Among the very darkest we know of.
Nothing about this world is friendly.

Imagine standing there, and seeing nothing at all.
Not darkness. Less than darkness.
You would never find the edge of the ground.

A small ring of dust still orbits it.
Leftovers from a system that no longer exists.

A whole sun's worth of wreckage, in one thin circle.
It circles nothing at all.
The dust keeps its shape out of pure habit.

You are watching it pass, and it will never know you.
And you will never get there.
It is the loneliest thing we have ever found.
